title_en: Annual Report on Intellectual Property Cases of the Supreme People's Court (Continued) (2009)
keywords_en: patent right; administrative litigation; objection to enforcement; intellectual property right; Supreme People's Court intellectual property case
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Intellectual Property Cases Annual Report (Continued)

(2009)

(Continued from previous issue)

41. Whether a judgment under execution may be terminated by ruling due to the patent being declared invalid

Where a party applies to terminate the execution of a patent infringement judgment that was rendered before the patent was declared invalid but has not yet been executed or has not been fully executed, based on a legally effective decision declaring the patent completely invalid, whether the people's court may terminate the execution is not explicitly provided for in Article 233 of the Civil Procedure Law.

In the case of a request for instructions from the Tianjin High People's Court on whether a judgment under execution should be terminated due to the patent being declared invalid [ (2009) Min San Ta Zi No. 13 ], the Supreme People's Court replied, holding that if a patent is declared invalid during the execution of an effective patent infringement judgment, the people's court shall rule to terminate the execution; if the party believes the original judgment is erroneous, it may seek relief through the trial supervision procedure.

The basic facts of this request for instructions case are as follows: In April 2008, the Tianjin High People's Court rendered a final judgment in a patent infringement case, finding the defendant liable for infringement and ordering it to compensate the plaintiff for losses. In June of the same year, the Patent Re-examination Board declared the patent completely invalid, and the patentee filed an administrative lawsuit against this decision. In September of the same year, the plaintiff applied for compulsory execution to the Tianjin No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, and the defendant objected to the execution on the ground that the patent had been declared invalid. In December of the same year, the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court ruled to uphold the invalidation decision of the Patent Re-examination Board; the parties did not appeal, and the administrative judgment became effective. However, the plaintiff still insisted that the court should enforce the execution, citing the explicit provisions of Article 47 of the Patent Law.

The Supreme People's Court replied, holding that where a judgment finding patent infringement has not been revoked, but the patent right found to be infringed in that judgment has been legally declared invalid, if the defendant could only apply to terminate the execution after revoking the original infringement judgment through the trial supervision procedure, this would not only waste procedural resources but also increase the litigation costs for the parties, which is not conducive to timely dispute resolution. Therefore, from the perspective of providing timely judicial relief to the parties, the provisions on termination of execution in the Civil Procedure Law may be interpreted appropriately, so that the executing court may directly rule to terminate the execution when a party applies for termination on the ground that the patent has been completely invalidated, without waiting for the revocation of the original enforcement basis. At the same time, the termination of execution does not prevent the defendant in the original infringement judgment from separately applying for revocation of the original infringement judgment through the trial supervision procedure.

42. Handling of new acts of implementation after the infringer has made changes to the original infringing technical solution

After a people's court's effective judgment confirms that a specific product or method constitutes infringement of another's patent right, the actor sometimes makes certain changes to the corresponding technical or design content involved in the infringement in their product or method and then implements it. In such cases, whether the actor's new acts of implementation fall within the scope of res judicata of the effective judgment and should be handled through execution proceedings, or whether they constitute a new subject matter of litigation requiring a new lawsuit, is often disputed in practice.

In the case of a request for instructions from the Sichuan High People's Court regarding the dispute over confirmation of non-infringement of patent rights filed by Sichuan Longsheng Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Longsheng Company) against Huainan Jieming Biomedical Research Institute (hereinafter referred to as Jieming Institute) [ (2009) Min San Ta Zi No. 6 ], the Supreme People's Court replied, holding that if the actor has substantially changed the corresponding technical or design content involved in the infringement in that product or method, the act of implementing the changed technology or design does not fall within the subject matter of execution of the original effective judgment and is not bound by the original effective judgment; whether it constitutes infringement should be determined by filing a separate lawsuit.

The basic facts of this request for instructions case are as follows: In January 2004, Jieming Institute filed a lawsuit in the Hefei Intermediate People's Court, Anhui Province, against Longsheng Company, alleging that the production method of "Liangjun Oral Liquid" (Chuan Wei Yao Jian Zi [95] No. 011116) infringed Jieming Institute's patent for "Production Method of Liangjun Syrup." In January 2005, the court ruled that Longsheng Company should stop using Jieming Institute's invention patent to produce and sell "Liangjun Oral Liquid" and compensate for economic losses. Longsheng Company appealed. The Anhui High People's Court upheld the first-instance judgment in the second instance. Subsequently, the Hefei Intermediate People's Court issued a notice of assistance in execution to the State Food and Drug Administration, requesting assistance in revoking Longsheng Company's drug approval number for "Liangjun Oral Solution." On February 25, 2009, the State Food and Drug Administration revoked Longsheng Company's drug approval number. Jieming Institute published a "Solemn Statement" on the Internet and disseminated propaganda in the Chengdu area, claiming that the "Liangjun Oral Solution" currently produced and sold by Longsheng Company infringed Jieming Institute's invention patent for "Production Method of Liangjun Syrup" and stating that it would pursue legal liability against Longsheng Company. Longsheng Company believed that its "Liangjun Oral Liquid" and "Liangjun Oral Solution" were two different products with different production methods, so it filed a lawsuit in the Chengdu Intermediate People's Court, Sichuan Province, seeking a declaration that its production method for "Liangjun Oral Solution" did not infringe the patent in question owned by Jieming Institute. The Sichuan High People's Court requested instructions from the Supreme People's Court on whether the case accepted by the Chengdu Intermediate People's Court constituted an independent lawsuit.

The Supreme People's Court replied, holding that after a people's court's effective judgment confirms that a specific product or method constitutes infringement of another's patent right, if the actor substantially changes the corresponding technical or design content involved in the infringement in that product or method, the act of implementing the changed technology or design does not fall within the subject matter of execution of the original effective judgment. Whether the actor's act of implementing the changed technology or design still constitutes infringement of the patent right should be determined by filing a separate lawsuit. If the actor refuses to perform the obligation to cease the infringement as determined in the effective judgment of the people's court and continues the original infringing act, the right holder may, in addition to requesting the relevant authorities to pursue the actor's legal liability for refusing to execute the judgment or ruling, also file a separate lawsuit to pursue civil liability for the continued infringing act.

43. Handling of applications for retrial where the original judgment is indeed erroneous but the parties have already reached a settlement agreement

According to the provisions of the Civil Procedure Law on trial supervision procedures, if the original judgment is indeed erroneous, the case should be brought up for trial or remanded for retrial. In retrial review cases, sometimes the original judgment is indeed erroneous, but the parties have already reached a settlement agreement. In such cases, initiating retrial proceedings would not only cause procedural inefficiency but also hinder the parties' willingness to settle and the execution of the settlement.

In the case of the application for retrial filed by the complainant Shanghai Bifengtang Food Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Bifengtang Company) against the respondent Shanghai Dongyongmatou Catering Management Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Dongyongmatou Company) regarding an unfair competition dispute [ (2007) Min San Jian Zi No. 21-1 ], the Supreme People's Court attempted to innovate the review and handling methods for retrial review cases. Where the original judgment was indeed erroneous but the parties had reached a settlement agreement, the court made a clear review determination of the errors in the original judgment in the ruling granting the withdrawal of the retrial application. This avoided the procedural inefficiency caused by initiating a retrial to correct the erroneous determination in the original judgment, and also reflected the judicial policy orientation of encouraging and facilitating the settlement of civil disputes through party agreement.

The basic facts of this case are as follows: Bifengtang Company was registered and established on September 15, 1998, engaged in catering services. It subsequently opened several branches in Shanghai. The menus, food packaging boxes, and printed calendars used by Bifengtang Company and its branches all bore the characters "避风塘" and their Chinese pinyin. Bifengtang Company also received honors such as the 2000 Shanghai Commercial Quality Service Advanced Collective and the "Jing'an Nanjing Road Style Bar" Featured Landscape Award. Bifengtang Company's Shrimp Dumpling Emperor, Crispy Egg Tart King, and Egg Yolk White Lotus Seed Paste Mooncakes were respectively recognized by the China Cuisine Association as Chinese Famous Snacks and as high-quality mooncakes at the "2001 National Catering Industry Mooncake Exhibition and Catering Food and Enterprise Showcase." Newspapers and periodicals such as Xinmin Evening News and Reader Guide had reported on Bifengtang Company and its branches and had published advertisements for Bifengtang Company. Dongyongmatou Company was registered and established on August 7, 2001, originally named "Shanghai Xuhui Fisheries Causeway Bay Catering Management Co., Ltd.," and changed its name to "Shanghai Dongyongmatou Catering Management Co., Ltd." upon approval on January 25, 2002, also engaged in catering services. The storefront signs and outdoor advertisements of Dongyongmatou Company bore the characters "东涌码头避风塘" and "避风塘料理." The menus used by Dongyongmatou Company had the characters "渔家铜锣湾" at the top and the slogan "走进渔家铜锣湾享受原味避风塘" at the bottom. Bifengtang Company filed a lawsuit alleging that Dongyongmatou Company infringed on its renowned service's distinctive name and enterprise name and also constituted false advertising. The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held at first instance that Dongyongmatou Company had not used "避风塘" as a character in its enterprise name, would not cause consumer misunderstanding or confusion, and did not constitute infringement of the plaintiff's enterprise name rights; the term "避风塘" was not originally created by Bifengtang Company but had gradually become a name accepted by consumers as a type of characteristic flavor cuisine and dining style; the defendant's use of "避风塘料理" and similar terms in advertisements did not constitute false advertising; the term "避风塘" was not first used by Bifengtang Company in catering business activities and, as a name widely used by operators in the catering industry to represent a type of characteristic flavor cuisine and dining style, could not be exclusively enjoyed by the plaintiff as a service name. The court thus ruled to reject the plaintiff's claims. After Bifengtang Company appealed, the Shanghai High People's Court held in the second instance that "避风塘" had not only its original meaning of a small sheltered harbor but had also become the name of a unique cooking method and the characteristic flavor dishes made by that method. Based on this, the court dismissed the appeal. Bifengtang Company then applied for retrial to the Shanghai High People's Court, which was notified and rejected. Bifengtang Company remained dissatisfied and appealed to the Supreme People's Court. During the review, the Supreme People's Court additionally found the following facts: The complainant held a "China Famous Catering Enterprise" plaque issued by the China Cuisine Association in November 2002, bearing the title "Shanghai Bifengtang"; in the catering industry, operators commonly use terms such as "Bifengtang Fried Crab," "Bifengtang Fried Shrimp," and "Bifengtang Eggplant" as names representing characteristic flavor dishes. During the review period of the Supreme People's Court, the parties voluntarily reached a settlement agreement, in which the respondent acknowledged that "避风塘" had become the complainant's distinctive service name due to long-term use and widespread promotion, and the respondent had ceased and guaranteed not to use the term "避风塘" in advertising in the future. Based on the above settlement agreement, the complainant immediately applied to withdraw its complaint. On December 31, 2009, the Supreme People's Court ruled to grant Bifengtang Company's withdrawal of its complaint.

The Supreme People's Court held in its review that the above settlement agreement was voluntarily reached by the parties, did not involve harm to national interests, social public interests, or the interests of third parties, did not violate the parties' true intent, and did not violate any prohibitive provisions of laws or administrative regulations. Regarding the issue in the agreement that both parties recognized "避风塘" as the distinctive name of the complainant's renowned service, although this differed from the relevant determination of the original court, based on the existing evidence in this case and the relevant facts found by the original court and this court, it could be recognized. First, it could be determined that the catering services provided by the complainant in the Shanghai area constituted renowned services, and the parties had no substantive dispute on this point in the original trial or during the review by this court. Second, although the term "避风塘" had its original meaning of a "sheltered harbor for ships" in the geographical sense, and was also used by catering operators as a generic name for specific dishes when combined with ingredients to indicate characteristic flavor dishes, through the complainant's long-term use in its enterprise name and widespread promotion in the sense of a commercial identifier, in the Shanghai area's catering service industry, "避风塘" had also acquired the function of identifying the operator's identity and could indicate the source of specific catering services. The determination by the court of second instance that "避风塘" had become the name of a unique cooking method and the characteristic flavor dishes made by that method was not supported by sufficient evidence. In this case, it could be determined that "避风塘" was the distinctive name of the complainant's well-known catering services in the Shanghai area. Third, the respondent had used the characters "东涌码头避风塘料理" and "避风塘料理" on its storefront signs and outdoor billboards, and had used the advertising slogan "走进渔家铜锣湾享受原味避风塘" on its menus. These uses effectively highlighted the term "避风塘," not used in its geographical sense or as a specific dish name, but as an identity marker, which could easily cause consumer confusion and misidentification with the complainant, exceeding the scope of fair use of the term "避风塘." Therefore, the respondent had actually ceased and promised in the settlement agreement not to use the term "避风塘" in the above manner, reflecting respect for the complainant's relevant civil rights and interests.

44. Determination of the validity of a jurisdictional agreement in foreign-related contracts

Article 242 of the Civil Procedure Law provides that parties to a dispute over a foreign-related contract or foreign-related property rights and interests may agree in writing to choose a court that has actual connection with the dispute. Whether the above provision should be interpreted as an authorization norm or a directive norm directly affects the determination of the validity of the parties' jurisdictional agreement.

In the case of a jurisdictional objection to a dispute over an online game agency and licensing contract between the appellant Korean MGAME Corporation (hereinafter referred to as MGAME Company) and the respondent Shandong Jufeng Network Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Jufeng Network Company), and the third party at first instance Tianjin Fengyun Network Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Fengyun Network Company) [ (2009) Min San Zhong Zi No. 4 ], the Supreme People's Court held that the validity of an agreement selecting a court should be determined according to the law of the forum; Article 242 of the Civil Procedure Law, which provides that parties "may agree in writing to choose a court that has actual connection with the dispute," should, based on the legislative background and relevant legislative intent at the time, be interpreted as an authorization norm rather than a directive norm; when parties to a foreign-related contract or foreign-related property rights and interests dispute agree to choose a court, they should choose a court that has actual connection with the dispute; otherwise, the agreement choosing the court is invalid.

The basic facts of this case are as follows: Jufeng Network Company filed a lawsuit against MGAME Company as defendant, with Fengyun Network Company as a third party, based on the "Game Licensing Agreement" entered into between Jufeng Network Company and MGAME Company on March 25, 2005. MGAME Company raised a jurisdictional objection, arguing that the case should be heard by a competent court in Singapore. Its main ground was the provision of Article 21 of the agreement: "This Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of China. All disputes arising out of or in connection with this Agreement shall be finally settled in Singapore, and all disputes arising out of this Agreement shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Singapore." The Shandong High People's Court held upon review that since the parties chose Chinese law as the governing law for the agreement, the parties' jurisdictional agreement must also comply with the relevant provisions of the chosen governing law, i.e., Chinese law; in accordance with Article 242 of the Civil Procedure Law, the court chosen by the parties should be limited to a place that has actual connection with the dispute, and Singapore had no connection with the dispute; therefore, the agreed jurisdiction should be invalid. The court thus ruled to dismiss the jurisdictional objection. After MGAME Company appealed, the Supreme People's Court ruled on December 22, 2009 to dismiss the appeal and uphold the original ruling.

The Supreme People's Court held in its trial that, according to Article 145 of the General Principles of the Civil Law and Article 242 of the Civil Procedure Law, as well as Article 1 of the Supreme People's Court's Provisions on Several Issues concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Foreign-Related Civil or Commercial Contract Disputes, choosing the applicable law and choosing the jurisdictional court are two entirely different legal acts, and their validity should be determined separately according to the relevant legal provisions. The validity of an agreement selecting a court should be determined according to the law of the forum; the original court's ruling that the jurisdictional agreement must comply with the relevant legal provisions of the country to which the chosen governing law belongs was erroneous. Regarding the issue of parties to foreign-related cases choosing a court through agreement, the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (for Trial Implementation), which came into effect on October 1, 1982, did not make special provisions. The current provision was made in the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, which was promulgated and came into effect on April 9, 1991. Based on the legislative background and relevant legislative spirit at that time, the provision in that article that parties "may agree in writing to choose a court that has actual connection with the dispute" should be interpreted as an authorization norm, not a directive norm. That is, when parties to a foreign-related contract or foreign-related property rights and interests dispute agree to choose a court, they should choose a court that has actual connection with the dispute; otherwise, the agreement choosing the court is invalid. At the same time, such an agreement choosing a court may be made in advance or subsequently, but must be fixed and confirmed in some written form. Accordingly, under the current legal provisions of China, the requirement of written form and actual connection remains for the selection of a court by agreement in foreign-related contract or foreign-related property rights and interests disputes. In this case, Singapore, agreed upon by the parties, is neither the domicile of the parties, nor the place of performance of the contract, nor the place of contract signing, nor the location of the subject matter. Furthermore, the applicable law chosen by the parties in this case is not Singaporean law, and the appellant could not prove that Singapore has any other actual connection with the dispute. Therefore, it should be held that Singapore has no actual connection with the dispute. Accordingly, the provision in Article 21 of the contract regarding jurisdiction over disputes is invalid and cannot serve as the basis for determining jurisdiction in this case.

Conclusion

Compiling the Annual Report on Intellectual Property Cases represents both a new endeavor by the Supreme People's Court to summarize its own trial experience, innovate methods of trial guidance, and unify the standards for the application of law, and a major measure to promote judicial transparency and accept oversight from all sectors. The elucidation of legal issues in these cases serves as a demonstration and guidance for judges hearing intellectual property cases, and provides direction and significance for the relevant public. At the same time, it should be noted that the aforementioned cases reflect the Supreme People's Court's understanding and exploration of issues concerning the application of law in specific cases in 2009, which may be subject to the specific circumstances of the individual cases, the cognitive level of the judges, and even the state of social, economic, technological, and cultural development at that time. The adjudication process for new, complex, and difficult cases is an exploratory process aimed at fairness and efficiency, and is a developmental process that keeps pace with the times. In this process, one must not adhere to conventions, but must continuously innovate based on a proper grasp of new developments in the country and society as well as the new judicial needs of the people. In this process, the Supreme People's Court will continuously study and explore, responding to the judicial needs of the people more timely and effectively, and serving the overall development of the country and society more proactively. The Supreme People's Court will also make the publication of the Annual Report on Intellectual Property Cases a routine practice, turning it into an important vehicle for guiding China's intellectual property trial work and a significant window for the public to understand the intellectual property trial work of the Supreme People's Court.

(End)
